service_ops.subtitle: Complete our comprehensive assessment to discover your professional strengths

q1.question: When service metrics dip, your first step is to:
options: Segment by shift/location
Check process compliance
Compare with historical patterns
Verify data integrity

q2.question: A process change you've implemented is causing confusion among frontline staff. Some are reverting to old procedures. You can't mandate compliance without understanding the breakdown. How do you diagnose and address the communication gap?
options: Reissue the procedure documentation with step-by-step detail, numbered exceptions, and explicit comparisons to the old process
Explain the why behind the change — connect the new process to outcomes staff care about, rather than reissuing the how
Spend a shift observing where staff revert, ask them what's unclear in their own words, then revise communication based on actual confusion points
Replace written instructions with a short walkthrough video showing the new process in context, supplemented by a quick-reference card

q3.question: Your team follows a standard procedure, but an unusual case doesn't fit the existing protocol. The procedure manual doesn't cover this scenario. You:
options: Identify which parts of the standard procedure still apply and adapt the rest with documented reasoning
Consult a colleague who's handled similar edge cases to understand how they approached it
Escalate to a supervisor with a clear description of why the standard procedure doesn't fit
Handle it using your best judgment and write up the case so the procedure can be updated

q4.question: Your service team needs to reduce average handling time by 20%, but cutting steps would hurt quality scores. You can't hire more staff. You:
options: Redesign the service flow so that common cases follow a streamlined path while complex cases get the full process — handling both faster on average
Identify the most time-consuming step and find a way to perform it in parallel with another step rather than sequentially
Redefine 'handling time' by shifting some steps to asynchronous follow-up, reducing live interaction time without cutting content
Create templated responses for the most frequent 30% of requests, freeing agents to spend more time on the remaining complex cases

q5.question: Your team's incident response time has been slower than the target, and you are part of the problem. You:
options: Shadow the fastest responder on shift and document what they do differently
Review your last five incidents to find the specific step where you lost time
Practice responding to simulated incidents with a timer to build speed
Redesign your personal triage checklist based on what has actually slowed you down

q6.question: To schedule staff effectively, you:
options: Model demand by hour
Account for skill mix
Plan buffers for spikes
Review constraints and rules

q7.question: A customer is escalating a complaint. They're factually wrong about what happened, but emotionally they've had a genuinely poor experience. Your response will be reviewed by your manager. How do you handle the factual inaccuracy while addressing the experience?
options: Acknowledge their frustration, then walk through what actually occurred with timestamps and specifics — clarity prevents future disputes
Focus the response on the experience gap rather than the factual sequence — 'regardless of specifics, the outcome fell short' — and propose resolution
Ask the customer to confirm specific details of their experience — let them self-correct factual errors through clarifying questions rather than direct contradiction
Respond in writing with empathy and resolution, then offer a phone call to discuss details — verbal exchange reduces the adversarial dynamic of written correction

q8.question: Two experienced team members give you contradictory advice on handling a service situation. Both have strong track records. You:
options: Ask each to explain the reasoning behind their recommendation, not just the conclusion
Look at what's different about this situation compared to when each approach worked before
Try the approach with the lower downside risk and evaluate the outcome
Check if there's a documented precedent for this type of situation before deciding

q9.question: A key supplier notifies you that a critical component will be unavailable for three weeks. Your service depends on it daily. Switching suppliers permanently isn't viable due to contracts. You:
options: Source a temporary alternative that covers the gap, even if it's not identical, and adjust your process to accommodate the differences
Redesign the affected service workflow to function without the component for three weeks, even if it means a different (but acceptable) customer experience
Negotiate with the supplier to provide partial or substitute deliveries, prioritizing the specific variants you need most urgently
Build a small reserve by reducing usage in lower-priority applications and redirecting inventory to the most critical service lines

q10.question: Customer feedback shows that your team's explanations during outages are confusing — and you wrote the scripts. You:
options: Record real explanations and review them to identify what is unclear
Practice with mock scenarios using plain-language scripts until it feels natural
Ask a communication trainer to observe one interaction and give targeted advice
Create a template library for common outage explanations and test it with users

q11.question: To reduce errors, you:
options: Introduce checklists
Standardize and 5S
Automate repetitive steps
Trace each error back to the step where it first appears

q12.question: You need to communicate a service-level reduction to long-term clients. The reduction is permanent and non-negotiable. Some clients will be significantly impacted. You must preserve the relationship while being transparent. How do you deliver the message?
options: State the change clearly with effective dates and specific impacts per client segment — ambiguity would be worse than bad news
Frame within a broader service evolution narrative — position the reduction as part of a strategic shift that includes improvements in other areas
Contact the most impacted clients individually first, gauge their concerns, then use those insights to refine the broader announcement
Replace a mass announcement with individual account reviews — each client hears the news in the context of their specific relationship and usage

q13.question: You've relied on an operational procedure for months. A junior team member presents preliminary case data suggesting one of its core assumptions is wrong. You:
options: Pause applying the procedure in affected cases and test both approaches on recent cases before committing either way
Review the team member's raw case data yourself to assess its strength before involving anyone else
Note the challenge formally and continue with the procedure, but define a specific outcome threshold that would trigger a full reassessment
Ask two people who weren't involved in either analysis to independently evaluate the conflicting evidence

q14.question: Management wants to introduce a digital self-service channel to reduce call volume by 30%. But your data shows that 60% of customers who try self-service end up calling anyway because the issues are too complex. You:
options: Redesign the self-service flow to handle only the cases it can actually resolve well, and route complex cases to agents faster rather than trying to contain them
Create a hybrid: let customers start in self-service but offer a seamless escalation that preserves context, so the agent call is shorter
Reframe the 30% target: instead of reducing total calls, focus on reducing repeat calls by using self-service for follow-ups and status checks
Pilot three different self-service approaches on different case types to identify which categories actually benefit from automation before scaling

q15.question: An audit found that your compliance documentation has recurring gaps — a skill you haven't developed. You:
options: Identify the two most common gaps and create a personal checklist for those areas
Ask the auditor to walk you through exactly what good documentation looks like
Compare your documentation with a colleague's who scored well, side by side
Redo one recent document from scratch using the correct standard and time yourself

q16.question: Choosing a new tool, you:
options: Score by requirements fit
Pilot with a small group
Evaluate cost/benefit and risk
Check integration with systems

q17.question: You've been asked to train a new team on a complex workflow. Half the group has operational experience in a related field; the other half are complete beginners. You have one training session. How do you structure it?
options: Teach the full workflow end-to-end at beginner level, then offer an advanced supplement session for experienced members who want deeper context
Start with the conceptual model — why the workflow exists — then let experienced members connect it to what they know while beginners build from scratch
Begin with a diagnostic exercise that reveals what each person already knows, then adjust depth dynamically based on actual gaps
Pair experienced and beginner members, provide a guided practice scenario, and circulate to address individual questions — replace lecture with structured peer learning

q18.question: A new industry guideline contradicts a practice your team has used successfully for years. The guideline's evidence base is limited but growing. You:
options: Review the evidence behind the guideline and compare it with your team's outcome data
Pilot the new guideline on a subset of cases while maintaining the old practice as control
Adopt the guideline but track outcomes closely to verify it performs as claimed
Consult peers at other organizations to understand how they're interpreting and implementing it

q19.question: Your team runs a 24/7 operation. A new regulation requires additional documentation at each handoff between shifts, but adding paperwork would slow transitions and create a 15-minute gap in coverage. You:
options: Redesign the handoff format: replace the paper-based approach with a structured digital log that auto-populates from the shift's activity data
Overlap shifts by 15 minutes and use the overlap period for both handoff and documentation, absorbing the time cost within the schedule
Split the documentation requirement: capture critical items during the handoff and defer detailed notes to a quieter period within the next shift
Redefine the documentation scope: work with compliance to identify the minimum viable documentation that satisfies the regulation without the full burden

q20.question: You've been told your process improvement proposals lack data support — a skill you haven't developed. You:
options: Attach measurable baselines to your next proposal, even if the data collection takes extra time
Partner with an analyst to learn how they build data-backed arguments
Take a short course on operational data analysis and apply it to a real improvement case
Review three approved proposals to reverse-engineer what data made them convincing

q21.question: Evaluating a process change, you:
options: Define success metrics up front
Compare before/after data
Run a controlled trial
Document impact and next steps

open1.question: Describe a time you improved a service process. What changed and how did you make it stick?

open2.question: What area of your operations practice do you most want to grow this year, and what's your plan?

q1.title: Your first move with a complex data set
q1.body:
You have a large, messy data set in front of you: the question asks what you would actually do first.

**A.** You split the data into smaller parts (by period, source or type) and look at one part at a time.

**B.** You look at the data as a whole straight away, searching for trends, peaks or recurring patterns.

**C.** Before analysing, you pick tools or software (a spreadsheet, a script, a BI tool) that can do the heavy lifting.

**D.** You first consult someone who has worked with similar data and ask how they approached it.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q2.title: Presenting a simulation to a mixed committee
q2.body:
You have 20 minutes to present your simulation to experts and non-technical funders: the question asks how you would actually structure it.

**A.** You walk through the methodology step by step with the technical evidence, and give executives a detailed appendix to read afterwards.

**B.** You open with what the results mean for funding decisions and only go into methodology when an expert asks about it.

**C.** You spend the first two minutes asking what each subgroup wants from the session, then decide how deep to go.

**D.** Two days before, you send the experts the technical paper and use the meeting only for the executives' decision.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q3.title: A limitation in a well-cited paper, due tomorrow
q3.body:
The team's decision relies on a widely cited paper whose method has a limitation only you have spotted, and the deadline is tomorrow: the question asks what you would actually do.

**A.** You raise the limitation with the team today and suggest a quick check of how much the result changes if the key assumption shifts.

**B.** You go ahead with the paper's conclusions and write a note describing the limitation so it can be revisited later.

**C.** You look for an independent study that reached its results with a different methodology and compare the two.

**D.** You ask a colleague who knows the field well whether the limitation actually affects your specific case.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q4.title: A pipeline bottleneck and a library not ready
q4.body:
The fix you want needs a library due in three months, but the deadline is in six weeks: the question asks what you would actually do.

**A.** You combine two stable libraries to get close to what the new one would do, accepting somewhat slower performance.

**B.** You change how data moves through the pipeline so it no longer passes through the stage that causes the bottleneck.

**C.** You write a small version of the critical feature yourself, built so it can be removed once the library is released.

**D.** You propose delivering part of the work now with current tools and the rest when the library is ready.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q5.title: Debugging that keeps failing on distributed errors
q5.body:
Your usual way of debugging keeps failing on a new type of distributed-system error: the question asks what you would actually do about it.

**A.** You sit next to someone who knows these errors well while they debug and follow each step of their method.

**B.** You block out a fixed slot every week to reproduce these errors and work through them one by one.

**C.** After each failed attempt you add an item to a checklist of what you missed, so the gaps become visible over time.

**D.** You try a completely different debugging framework on the same errors and compare what each one finds.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q6.title: How you judge whether a technical solution works
q6.body:
A technical solution has been built and you need to decide whether it does its job: the question asks what you would actually check first.

**A.** You measure concrete numbers such as response time, error rate or resource use and compare them with a target.

**B.** You set the solution against one or two alternatives, for example with an A/B test on real traffic.

**C.** You gather feedback from the users who work with it day to day on what helps them and what gets in the way.

**D.** You go through the list of requirements one by one and verify that each is met.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q7.title: A senior engineer challenges you in jargon
q7.body:
In a review, a senior engineer challenges your data interpretation in jargon few people follow, and the room goes quiet: the question asks how you would actually respond.

**A.** You answer the engineer's technical points in the same technical terms first, and only then explain the exchange to everyone else.

**B.** You first restate the engineer's concern in plain words for the whole room, then answer at that level.

**C.** You ask the engineer which specific data point they are questioning, which also gives you a moment to read the room.

**D.** You acknowledge the point publicly, offer to continue the technical discussion later and bring the meeting back to shared topics.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q8.title: Two reliable sources that disagree
q8.body:
Two data sources that have always been reliable now give opposite readings on a system's health: the question asks what you would actually do.

**A.** You check the measurement conditions of each source (timing, location, load) to find what could explain the difference.

**B.** You give more weight to the source that has been right more often in similar situations.

**C.** You run your own independent diagnostic test to get a third reading to compare with the other two.

**D.** You contact the teams that maintain each source and ask whether anything changed recently in their calibration.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q9.title: A monitoring system with 60% of the sensors
q9.body:
The budget covers only 60% of the sensors you planned, and less coverage means blind spots: the question asks what you would actually do.

**A.** You place the sensors you can afford in the high-risk zones and use statistical estimates to fill in the areas without them.

**B.** You put cheaper, less precise sensors in non-critical areas and higher-grade ones only where accuracy matters most.

**C.** You change the goal from covering everything to detecting anomalies, so the system alerts only when readings move away from the usual baseline.

**D.** You install what the budget pays for now, on a modular setup that lets you add more sensors later.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q10.title: The same design weakness in every code review
q10.body:
Code reviews keep pointing out the same design weakness and you haven't fixed it yet: the question asks what you would actually do next.

**A.** You ask the reviewer to show you, directly on your own code, how they would structure it differently.

**B.** You take an old module and rewrite it with the recommended pattern until it feels natural.

**C.** You set a concrete target, such as no comments on that issue, for your next three pull requests.

**D.** You read up on the design principle behind the comments before writing more code.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q11.title: Your approach to automating repetitive work
q11.body:
A task repeats every day or week and could be automated: the question asks how you would actually go about it.

**A.** You spot the patterns that repeat and write custom scripts for them, for example in Python.

**B.** You start from a tool you already have, such as a spreadsheet macro or an integration, and adapt it to the task.

**C.** Before building anything, you weigh the cost of the hours saved against the time needed to automate and maintain it.

**D.** You collaborate with a developer or IT colleague so they can implement the automation with you.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q12.title: A critical flaw 48 hours before an audit
q12.body:
Two days before an audit you find a critical flaw and must inform three people in writing within the hour: the question asks how you would actually handle it.

**A.** You write one full incident report covering technical cause, legal exposure and operational steps, and send it to all three.

**B.** You draft three separate messages: technical detail for your manager, risk for compliance, an action checklist for operations.

**C.** You send all three a short alert stating how serious it is, then ask each of them what they need before writing more.

**D.** You send a short written alert so there is a record, then immediately ask for a 15-minute call with all three.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q13.title: A junior colleague questions your framework
q13.body:
A junior colleague brings early evidence that a core assumption of the framework you've used for months is wrong: the question asks what you would actually do.

**A.** You stop using the framework for now and test both versions of the assumption on recent data before deciding.

**B.** You go through the colleague's raw evidence on your own to judge how solid it is before bringing anyone else in.

**C.** You record the objection formally and keep using the framework, setting a specific threshold that would lead you to reassess it fully.

**D.** You ask two people who worked on neither analysis to look at the conflicting evidence independently.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q14.title: A contract feature that harms the architecture
q14.body:
The contract requires a feature that works but would make the system's architecture harder to develop further: the question asks how you would actually build it.

**A.** You implement it behind a separate abstraction layer, so it can later be swapped out without touching the rest of the system.

**B.** You propose a different technical route that gives the client the same result while keeping the architecture intact.

**C.** You build it exactly as specified and, at the same time, write a document explaining how to refactor it later.

**D.** You negotiate: deliver the core of what the client needs in a cleaner form and postpone the parts that would do the most damage.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q15.title: After an incident exposed a monitoring gap
q15.body:
A production incident showed a gap in what you know about monitoring, and it is now resolved: the question asks what you would actually do next.

**A.** You write down exactly which signals you missed and add them to a personal checklist for future incidents.

**B.** You book time with the on-call engineer and go through what they noticed that you did not.

**C.** You set up a sandbox where you trigger similar failures on purpose and practise your response.

**D.** You rework the alert thresholds based on what you learned, then check over two weeks whether they fire when expected.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q16.title: Working through a large amount of data
q16.body:
You have a large volume of data to analyse: the question asks how you would actually start working through it.

**A.** You build charts or dashboards with visualization tools and look at them to spot patterns.

**B.** You split the data into logical groups, such as by customer, region or product, and handle each group separately.

**C.** You apply statistical methods, such as correlation or regression, to see which variables move together.

**D.** You first decide which subsets of the data could have the most impact and analyse those before the rest.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q17.title: Your model contradicts a partner team's
q17.body:
A partner team's validated model contradicts yours and the joint deliverable is due in five days: the question asks how you would actually open the first alignment meeting.

**A.** You show both models with their assumptions listed side by side and walk through the data before suggesting how to reconcile them.

**B.** You describe the gap as a difference in scope and steer the discussion to what the joint deliverable actually needs.

**C.** You ask the partner team to explain their reasoning first, listening for gaps before presenting your model.

**D.** You propose a shared document where both models sit side by side with labelled assumptions, instead of debating out loud.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q18.title: Vendor benchmarks that don't match your setup
q18.body:
A vendor shows impressive benchmarks for a new technology, but they were measured in conditions unlike your production environment: the question asks what you would actually do.

**A.** You set up a controlled test that reproduces your own data volumes, hardware and constraints.

**B.** You look for independent users who run it in conditions similar to yours and ask about their experience.

**C.** You list the differences between the vendor's test conditions and yours and estimate how performance would change.

**D.** You ask the vendor for their raw data and re-run the analysis with your own parameters.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q19.title: A new algorithm regulators may not follow
q19.body:
Your team's new algorithm beats the standard approach in testing, but regulators and stakeholders expect the conventional method: the question asks what you would actually do.

**A.** For a trial period you run both algorithms, report with the standard one and check the new one's results against it.

**B.** You keep the algorithm as it is and rewrite the explanation in the terms and structure the regulatory framework uses.

**C.** You build a hybrid on the structure of the standard method, adding your algorithm's key innovation where it counts most.

**D.** You propose adopting it in stages: the conventional approach stays in regulated areas while the new algorithm starts in less scrutinised uses.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q20.title: Months of difficulty with a technical area
q20.body:
You have been struggling with a technical area, such as performance optimisation, for months: the question asks what your actual next step would be.

**A.** You pick a small, specific project where you have to use that skill under real deadlines and limits.

**B.** Every week you note what you tried and what came of it, to see whether your approach is actually improving.

**C.** You ask someone experienced in the area for a frank view of what exactly you are doing wrong.

**D.** You change how you learn: if reading didn't help, you try building; if you worked alone, you try pairing.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q21.title: Assessing a new technology before adopting it
q21.body:
A new technology could be brought into your work: the question asks what you would actually look at first to decide.

**A.** You carry out a detailed cost-benefit analysis, putting figures on licences, training and migration against the expected gains.

**B.** You try it first on a small pilot project with a limited group before rolling it out everywhere.

**C.** You look at how it would change the existing processes and the daily work of the teams involved.

**D.** Before adopting it, you map its dependencies and possible failure modes, and what they would affect.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

open1.title: A moment of success in your work
open1.body:
Describe one specific professional situation rather than your career in general. A useful answer usually covers:

- the context and what was at stake
- what you personally did, as distinct from the team
- why it counts as a success for you (a result, feedback, something you learned)

A few sentences are enough, at least 50 characters. There is no right answer: what matters is that it is your own experience.

open2.title: An area where you want to grow
open2.body:
Name one concrete challenge or skill rather than a general wish. A useful answer usually covers:

- the area and why it matters in your work right now
- the concrete steps you are taking or plan to take
- how you will know it is working

A few sentences are enough, at least 50 characters. There is no right answer: describe honestly where you are now.

examplesByCategory.comp_power: These questions are about how you handle data, numbers and structured problems in technical and scientific work: where you start, how you break things down and how you check whether something works. Each option is a different way of working.
examplesByCategory.communication: These questions describe situations in technical and scientific work where you have to explain something, give news or deal with disagreement, often with different audiences at once. They ask how you would actually organise and deliver the message.
examplesByCategory.knowledge: These questions are about what you do when information in technical and scientific work is incomplete, contradictory or new to you: how you check it, whom you ask and when you decide.
examplesByCategory.creativity: These questions put you in front of a constraint in technical and scientific work (time, budget, rules, conflicting requests) and ask how you would find a way through it.
examplesByCategory.drive: These questions describe a skill gap or a setback in technical and scientific work and ask what concrete steps you would take next to improve.

q1.title: Your first step on a KPI dashboard
q1.body:
You open a dashboard of business KPIs: the question asks what you would actually do first.

**A.** You scan the figures against their targets and note which ones are clearly off.

**B.** You drill into the breakdown by segment (region, product, customer type) before looking at the totals.

**C.** You compare this period's numbers with previous months or years to see the trend.

**D.** You export the data to a spreadsheet so you can investigate it offline at your own pace.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q2.title: Preparing a 30-minute board pitch for a pivot
q2.body:
You have 30 minutes to win board approval for a strategic pivot, and each member focuses on something different: choose how you would actually prepare.

**A.** You build one complete deck that goes through financials, mission and risk mitigation in order, leaving nothing out.

**B.** You organise everything around the question "Why now?", so that numbers, mission and risk all feed a single story.

**C.** Beforehand you meet the CFO and the sceptical directors one to one, then use the board session only for the objections still open.

**D.** You send a memo with the full analysis three days before and spend the live slot entirely on questions.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q3.title: A market assumption put in doubt
q3.body:
Your strategy rests on a market assumption backed by a single analyst report, and a competitor's move now casts doubt on it: choose what you would actually do.

**A.** You ask someone outside the original report to run a quick, independent analysis of the assumption.

**B.** You rework the strategy so it still holds whether the original or the alternative assumption turns out true.

**C.** You call a few frontline salespeople and ask what they hear from customers about the market.

**D.** You write down the uncertainty and set a concrete trigger (a figure, a date) that would make you revisit the assumption.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q4.title: Entering a new segment in six months
q4.body:
Your company has to gain traction in a new market segment within six months, with a product not designed for it: choose what you would actually do.

**A.** You keep the product as it is but change its positioning, pricing and onboarding to speak the new segment's language.

**B.** You find a company already serving that segment and offer your product as an integrated add-on to their solution.

**C.** You launch a reduced version that covers only the use case where your product and the new segment's needs overlap most.

**D.** You look for a niche inside the new segment where the current product already fits, and grow outward from there.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q5.title: After a board presentation that fell flat
q5.body:
Your last board presentation fell flat because the financial story lacked depth: choose what you would actually do next.

**A.** You ask a CFO you trust to go through your next deck and point out the specific weak spots.

**B.** You rebuild the same presentation from scratch with a different narrative structure, for example starting from the conclusion.

**C.** You study three board decks you consider exemplary and list the techniques you are not yet using.

**D.** Before the next board, you present to a small internal group and collect feedback on the spot.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q6.title: Revenue drops with no obvious cause
q6.body:
Revenue is falling and the cause is not clear: choose what you would actually check first.

**A.** You split revenue by channel and by customer cohort to see where the drop is concentrated.

**B.** You line up the dates of the drop with recent price changes or promotions.

**C.** You check that tracking and attribution are working correctly before trusting the figures.

**D.** You benchmark the drop against seasonality, comparing it with the same period in previous years to see how much is due to seasonality.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q7.title: Announcing new roles after a restructure
q7.body:
After a restructure, the people in your team react in different ways and you must present their new responsibilities in a meeting: choose how you would actually approach it.

**A.** You present the new structure with each role, reporting line and timeline spelled out, so no one is unsure who does what.

**B.** In the meeting you talk about what the team as a whole must achieve, then discuss individual role changes one to one.

**C.** You open by asking each person what they most need clarified, then run the meeting around those questions.

**D.** You send written role descriptions before the meeting and keep the session itself for questions and concerns.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q8.title: Entering a market with contradictory data
q8.body:
You are entering a market where data is scarce and contradictory and experts disagree on the basics: choose what you would actually do.

**A.** You run a small pilot (a few customers, one region) to generate your own data before committing further.

**B.** You map where the experts disagree and note which piece of evidence would settle each point.

**C.** You follow the expert whose reasoning is easiest to trace, while watching for signals that contradict it.

**D.** You build two separate business cases, one for each of the two most plausible scenarios.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q9.title: A competitor launches your feature first
q9.body:
Two weeks before a key launch, your main competitor releases an almost identical feature with plenty of press coverage: choose what you would actually do.

**A.** You keep the date but change the launch message, centring it on a value the competitor did not address.

**B.** You speed up one capability only you offer, accepting less polish on the features both products share.

**C.** You pair the launch with an extra offer, such as a free trial or an integration, so the comparison happens on different terms.

**D.** You move the launch back one week to add a small, visible differentiator and prepare a counter-narrative.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q10.title: Improving how you run planning sessions
q10.body:
Your team's strategic planning output is weaker than other teams' and you suspect it comes from how you facilitate: choose what you would actually do.

**A.** You sit in on a colleague's strategy session and take structured notes on how they run it.

**B.** You record your next session and afterwards list what you would change.

**C.** You bring in an external facilitator for one session and take part as an observer to learn the technique.

**D.** You redesign your planning template around what produced weak output last time.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q11.title: Checking a price change before deciding
q11.body:
You are evaluating a pricing change: choose how you would actually assess it.

**A.** You run sensitivity analyses in a spreadsheet to see how margin and volume shift at different prices.

**B.** You A/B test two or more price points with real customers and compare the results.

**C.** You model price elasticity separately for each customer segment.

**D.** You validate the change through interviews with a handful of customers.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q12.title: Answering a client escalation to the CEO
q12.body:
A key client complained to your CEO, mixing real service gaps with wrong assumptions about your process, and you draft the reply: choose how you would actually handle the inaccuracies.

**A.** You address each point with facts: admit the valid gaps, correct the inaccuracies with evidence, keep a plain professional tone.

**B.** You open by acknowledging the client's experience, then present the inaccurate points as areas where your process differs from expectations.

**C.** Your draft covers the legitimate gaps; you flag the inaccuracies to the CEO separately, suggesting how to correct them.

**D.** You suggest the CEO offer a call instead of a written reply, and clear up the inaccuracies in conversation.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q13.title: A junior challenges your strategic model
q13.body:
A junior team member brings preliminary evidence that a core assumption of the strategic model you have used for months is wrong: choose what you would actually do.

**A.** You pause work with the model and test both versions against recent market data before deciding.

**B.** You go through the raw evidence yourself to judge how solid it is before involving anyone else.

**C.** You record the challenge formally and keep using the model, with a specific trigger that would force a full reassessment.

**D.** You ask two people not involved in either analysis to evaluate the conflicting evidence independently.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q14.title: A client asks for 40% of engineering
q14.body:
A major client wants a custom feature that would take 40% of engineering capacity and put the roadmap at stake: choose what you would actually do.

**A.** You propose a more general version of the feature that serves both the client and the roadmap, even if it takes longer.

**B.** You give the client an interim workaround with existing capabilities and schedule the full feature for next quarter.

**C.** You reopen the quarterly plan, push back the roadmap items with the lowest impact and move that capacity to the client feature.

**D.** You dig into the client's underlying problem to see whether something you already have or are building could solve it.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q15.title: After a launch that missed on timing
q15.body:
A product launch underperformed because you misjudged market timing: choose what you would actually do next.

**A.** You interview five customers to find out which signals you read wrong.

**B.** You build a post-mortem framework that sets your original assumptions side by side with the actual data.

**C.** You spend time with someone who called the market correctly and ask them to walk you through their reasoning.

**D.** For the next product you run a smaller test launch to check timing before committing fully.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q16.title: How you build next quarter's forecast
q16.body:
You have to forecast next quarter: choose how you would actually build the forecast.

**A.** You blend a bottom-up estimate (deal by deal, team by team) with a top-down model based on the market, and reconcile the two.

**B.** You stress-test a few scenarios, such as losing a major client or a sharp price change.

**C.** You go through your assumptions with the sales team and adjust them to what they see in the pipeline.

**D.** You simulate capacity constraints (people, production, delivery) to see how much you can actually deliver.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q17.title: Delivering a resource decision to two teams
q17.body:
Two departments you oversee are in conflict over resources, each head blaming the other, and you must announce a decision neither will fully like: choose how you would actually deliver it.

**A.** You present the decision, with full reasoning and trade-offs, to both department heads at the same time.

**B.** You explain the decision through the organisational constraint that makes a compromise necessary, without judging either side's case.

**C.** You meet each head separately to preview the decision and gauge their reaction, then hold a joint session.

**D.** You communicate the decision in writing with a clear rationale, then offer each head a one-to-one follow-up conversation.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q18.title: An ambiguous new regulation
q18.body:
A regulatory change will affect your business, but its interpretation is unclear and industry peers read it differently: choose what you would actually do.

**A.** You bring in a legal specialist and test several interpretations against how your operations actually run.

**B.** You wait for an industry body to publish guidance, and meanwhile prepare contingency plans.

**C.** You apply the most conservative interpretation now and relax it as the rules become clearer.

**D.** You look at how similar ambiguities were resolved in the past to estimate the likely outcome.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q19.title: A new revenue stream on a small budget
q19.body:
Your core product has stopped growing and the board wants a new revenue stream, with an R&D budget of 15% of current spend: choose what you would actually do.

**A.** You list assets the company underuses, such as data, APIs or expertise, and package them as an offering for a different buyer.

**B.** You move the product boundary: a free feature becomes a premium tier, or some capabilities are sold as separate products.

**C.** You run three small, time-boxed experiments on different revenue ideas before putting budget behind any one of them.

**D.** You partner with a complementary company to co-develop a joint offering that neither could build alone on this budget.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q20.title: Working on how you delegate
q20.body:
You keep hearing that the way you delegate is slowing the team down: choose what you would actually do about it.

**A.** This week you pick one task you would normally keep, hand it over completely and note what happens.

**B.** You ask your direct reports what they need from you to take full ownership of their work.

**C.** You watch how a peer delegates: which tasks they hand off, at what point and with what instructions.

**D.** You switch from daily to weekly check-ins and track whether quality holds.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q21.title: Your first step on a transformation program
q21.body:
You are evaluating a transformation program: choose what you would actually do first.

**A.** You define the success metrics (what should change, by how much, by when) before anything else.

**B.** You pilot the program in one area and compare it with a control group that keeps working as before.

**C.** You assess the organisation's readiness for the change and the main risk areas before starting.

**D.** You study reference cases of similar programs in other companies.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

open1.title: A decision you are proud of and its trade-offs
open1.body:
Describe one real decision you took in a position of responsibility and explain the trade-offs behind it. A useful answer covers:

- the situation and what was at stake
- the options you weighed and what each would have cost
- what you chose and why
- what happened afterwards

A few sentences are enough (at least 50 characters). There is no right answer: what counts is your actual reasoning.

open2.title: The area you are working to grow in
open2.body:
Name one area where you want to grow in your current role and show how you are working on it. A useful answer covers:

- the specific area (a skill, a habit, a type of situation)
- why it matters for your work and your team
- the concrete steps you are taking now
- how you will know it is improving

A few sentences are enough (at least 50 characters). There is no right answer: be specific and honest.

examplesByCategory.knowledge: These questions are about what you do when information in business and team decisions is incomplete, contradictory or new to you: how you check it, whom you ask and when you decide.
examplesByCategory.creativity: These questions put you in front of a constraint in business and team decisions (time, budget, rules, conflicting requests) and ask how you would find a way through it.
examplesByCategory.drive: These questions describe a skill gap or a setback in business and team decisions and ask what concrete steps you would take next to improve.

q1.title: Your first check on campaign performance data
q1.body:
You have the performance data of a creative campaign in front of you: the question asks what you would actually look at first.

**A.** You put engagement figures (clicks, views, saves) next to the objectives in the brief and see where they fall short or go beyond them.

**B.** You compare how the same creative performs across formats and placements, for example stories versus feed or banner versus video.

**C.** You break the results down by audience segments, such as age, region or new versus returning users.

**D.** Before reading any number, you check measurement integrity: tracking tags, attribution windows and whether the data is complete.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q2.title: Production misread the tone of your concept
q2.body:
Production delivered a valid version of your concept with a different tone, and there is no time to redo it: the question asks how you would actually handle it.

**A.** You list the tonal elements that differ, each with a reference, and ask the team which ones they can adjust in time.

**B.** You explain how you want the audience to react and let the team find its own way to the right tone.

**C.** You first ask the team how they read the brief, to find where the interpretations split.

**D.** You make a quick side-by-side of intended and delivered versions, so the team reacts to images.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q3.title: Working in an unfamiliar visual language
q3.body:
A new project needs a visual style you don't know, with a vague brief and few references: the question asks what you would actually do first.

**A.** You collect the closest existing examples and work out the design principles behind them, such as grid, contrast or type.

**B.** You sketch a few quick experiments in the new style and show them for feedback before developing any of them.

**C.** You set up short conversations with the stakeholders and ask what they picture when they think of the look they want.

**D.** You take elements of your existing style, like a palette or a layout habit, and stretch them toward the new direction.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q4.title: A bold campaign under legal restrictions
q4.body:
A client wants a bold campaign, but legal rules out comparative claims and superlatives and requires existing brand elements: the question asks how you would actually approach it.

**A.** You build the concept around the required brand elements, turning the logo, colours or mascot into the centre of the idea.

**B.** You keep every message within the legal limits and make the work stand out through composition, pacing and tone.

**C.** You prepare three compliant concepts, from restrained to daring, and let the client choose.

**D.** You drop claims altogether and build the campaign around a story that aims to make people feel something.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q5.title: A client found your strategy too shallow
q5.body:
A client has rejected your work for lacking strategic depth, an area you know is weak: the question asks what you would actually do next.

**A.** You ask the client for a concrete example of work with the depth they expected and study what it does differently.

**B.** On your next project you work alongside a strategist and watch how they build the narrative from insight to message.

**C.** You rewrite the strategy section of the rejected brief yourself and ask someone for honest critique of the new version.

**D.** You set aside time each week for strategy exercises taken from another creative field, such as copywriting or product design.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q6.title: What you rely on to pick a visual
q6.body:
You need to choose the main visual for a campaign: the question asks which source you would actually rely on most.

**A.** You run A/B tests on two or three thumbnails with a small audience and keep the one that gets more clicks.

**B.** You look at heatmaps or eye-tracking results to see where attention lands on each option.

**C.** You check how similar visuals did in past campaigns and follow those historical patterns.

**D.** You look at recent user research, such as interviews or short surveys, to see how people describe the options.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q7.title: Client feedback that contradicts the brief
q7.body:
A client asks for changes that contradict the brief they approved, without noticing it: the question asks how you would actually handle this.

**A.** You open the original brief in the meeting, go through the conflicting points one by one and ask which direction they want now.

**B.** You say the project has evolved since the brief and treat the new request as a natural change in scope.

**C.** You ask the client to describe what they want now in their own words and point out the contradiction only if they don't spot it.

**D.** You make two quick mockups, one for each direction, and let the client pick by looking at them.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q8.title: Mixed reactions in early user tests
q8.body:
Early user tests of your creative direction give mixed results, with some people enthusiastic and others confused: the question asks what you would actually do next.

**A.** You split the responses by audience group, such as age or usage habits, to see whether the reactions depend on who answered.

**B.** You test a simplified version to see whether people are confused by the idea itself or by how it is executed.

**C.** You go back to the original research and reread it looking for nuances you may have missed.

**D.** You run a new round with fresh testers and a clearer protocol, for example the same tasks and questions for everyone.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q9.title: One identity for luxury and affordable markets
q9.body:
You are designing one visual identity for a brand that sells in both luxury and affordable markets: the question asks how you would actually approach it.

**A.** You define a few shared core elements, such as logo and typeface, and let colour, imagery and tone change by channel.

**B.** You look for what both audiences value emotionally, for example care or reliability, and build the identity around it instead of price.

**C.** You design the main identity for the larger market segment and create a separate sub-brand treatment for the other.

**D.** You mock up three different approaches and test them with people from both audiences before choosing.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q10.title: Catching up on motion design
q10.body:
Your motion design skills are below what the team expects, and it shows in your projects: the question asks what you would actually do about it.

**A.** You volunteer for a small internal project that needs motion work and agree on a deadline you can realistically meet.

**B.** You ask an experienced colleague to work with you on your next animation and comment on it as you go.

**C.** You follow a structured course and use each lesson on a real deliverable within two days.

**D.** You pick five motion pieces you admire and break down the techniques they use that you don't.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q11.title: How you split a production budget
q11.body:
You have a production budget to divide across creative assets: the question asks how you would actually decide where the money goes.

**A.** For each asset you estimate the cost and the expected lift in results, then compare the two in a simple spreadsheet.

**B.** You decide which assets should have the most impact and fund those first.

**C.** You first build a cheap prototype of each main idea and commit most of the budget only after checking it.

**D.** You look at which existing assets can be reused or adapted, for example reshooting a single scene or recropping images.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q12.title: Critiquing a junior's work in a group review
q12.body:
In a creative review with two senior colleagues present, a junior's work has significant problems despite a lot of effort: the question asks how you would actually give feedback.

**A.** You say plainly what works and what doesn't in the work and give specific directions for the revision.

**B.** You talk about what the brief requires and where the piece departs from it, rather than judging its quality.

**C.** You first ask the junior what they would change with another day, then build your comments on the gaps they name.

**D.** In the group you give only the main direction, then book a private session for detailed critique and questions.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q13.title: When a junior's data questions your direction
q13.body:
A junior designer brings early user data suggesting that one of your core aesthetic assumptions may be wrong: the question asks what you would actually do.

**A.** You pause the current direction and test both versions with a new audience sample before deciding.

**B.** You go through the junior's raw data yourself to check how solid it is before involving anyone else.

**C.** You record the challenge formally, keep going, and set a specific feedback threshold that would trigger a full review.

**D.** You ask two people outside both directions to look at the conflicting evidence independently.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q14.title: Turning a video campaign into static posters
q14.body:
At the final review the client asks for your video campaign as a static outdoor series, same deadline: the question asks how you would actually do it.

**A.** You pick the key visual moments from the video and turn them into static posters that tell the story in order.

**B.** You go back to the core insight and redesign the idea for posters from scratch, without starting from the video frames.

**C.** You adapt the key frames and add a scannable element, such as a QR code leading to a short animation.

**D.** You propose two phases: a quick version with existing assets now, and a version optimised for the medium two weeks later.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q15.title: Typography as your weakest area
q15.body:
A portfolio review shows that typography is consistently your weakest area: the question asks what you would actually do about it.

**A.** You take one past project, redo only the typography, and put the old and new versions side by side.

**B.** You ask a typography specialist to review your work and point out exactly what needs to improve.

**C.** For the next month you note every type choice you make, then look for mistakes that keep coming back.

**D.** On your next project you use only type, with no illustration or colour, to keep the focus on it.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q16.title: Unblocking a slow creative workflow
q16.body:
Your creative workflow has hit a bottleneck and work is piling up: the question asks what you would actually do first.

**A.** You time each step of the process, from brief to delivery, to find the slowest stage.

**B.** You redesign the sequence of steps to remove hand-offs, so files and approvals pass between fewer people.

**C.** You try out alternative tools and estimate how long the team would need to get past the learning curve.

**D.** You compare the cost and licensing terms of replacement tools with what you pay now.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q17.title: Testing alignment with another discipline
q17.body:
A collaborator from another discipline uses their own vocabulary, and you suspect you mean different things by the same words: the question asks how you would actually check.

**A.** You start a shared glossary for the project where each key term gets one agreed definition, so gaps show up in writing.

**B.** You set the words aside, ask what success looks like to them and compare concrete expectations.

**C.** In the next meeting you repeat their points back in your own vocabulary and watch whether they correct you or look confused.

**D.** You propose a joint session where you both sketch or prototype the idea, so intent is shown rather than described.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q18.title: The client's taste versus your research
q18.body:
A client is sure their audience wants a certain aesthetic, but your research points the other way: the question asks what you would actually do.

**A.** You suggest running both approaches as an A/B test on a small sample before full production.

**B.** You share your research openly and ask the client what evidence their view is based on.

**C.** You look for a creative solution that takes elements from both sides, for example the client's palette with the layout your research supports.

**D.** You write down both positions and agree on success criteria that will settle the question after launch.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q19.title: A new look that loses older customers
q19.body:
Your team's new visual concept works with younger people but puts off the brand's older customers, and the client wants both: the question asks how you would actually proceed.

**A.** You combine elements of the new concept and the existing visual language into a bridge between the two.

**B.** You use the new concept in acquisition channels such as social ads, and keep the familiar style in email and loyalty messages.

**C.** You change the existing visual language gradually, adding the new concept's principles across touchpoints.

**D.** You test the new concept with a controlled segment of older customers to see how much change they accept before a full rollout.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q20.title: Stuck at the same level in creative direction
q20.body:
You feel your creative direction skills have plateaued: the question asks what you would actually do to move forward.

**A.** You take on a project in a format or genre you have never worked in, such as a podcast or an exhibition.

**B.** You ask three peers you trust to each name one specific area where your direction could improve.

**C.** You put your recent work next to work from a year ago and list what has actually changed.

**D.** You set skill targets for each quarter, each tied to a concrete deliverable that shows progress.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q21.title: Checking asset quality at scale
q21.body:
You have to judge the quality of many creative assets at once: the question asks how you would actually go about it.

**A.** You first write down measurable criteria, such as legibility, use of brand colours and file specs, and judge every asset against them.

**B.** You review the assets in batches, using the same checklist for each one.

**C.** You test a sample of the assets with a small audience and see how they respond.

**D.** You automate the checks that can be automated, like sizes, formats or safe areas, and look at the rest by hand.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

open1.title: A piece of work that changed results
open1.body:
Describe one piece you created that made a visible or measurable difference. A useful answer includes:

- the context and what needed to change
- what you made and the choices behind it
- why you think it worked
- the result, with numbers or concrete feedback if you have them

A few sentences are enough (at least 50 characters). There is no right answer: choose a real example you know well.

open2.title: The creative skill you want to grow
open2.body:
Name one creative skill you want to improve this year. A useful answer includes:

- the skill and why it matters for your work
- the concrete steps you are taking or plan to take
- how you will know it is working

A few sentences are enough (at least 50 characters). There is no right answer: be specific about your own situation.

q1.title: Your first step when service metrics dip
q1.body:
Service numbers have dropped and the question asks what you would actually look at first.

**A.** You segment the figures by shift and by location to see where the drop is concentrated.

**B.** You check whether the team is following the process as written, for example by reviewing a sample of recent cases.

**C.** You compare this week's numbers with historical patterns, such as the same period last year or recurring seasonal dips.

**D.** You verify that the data itself is correct: that nothing is missing, duplicated or recorded differently than before.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q2.title: Staff reverting after a process change
q2.body:
A new process is causing confusion and some staff are going back to the old way: how would you find the communication gap?

**A.** You reissue the documentation with every step spelled out, the exceptions numbered and a side-by-side comparison with the old process.

**B.** You explain why the change was made, linking the new process to results the staff care about.

**C.** You spend a shift observing where people revert, ask them what is unclear, and then revise the message around those points.

**D.** You replace the written instructions with a short video of the new process in a real setting, plus a one-page quick-reference card.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q3.title: A case the procedure manual doesn't cover
q3.body:
An unusual case falls outside the standard protocol and the manual has nothing on it: you are asked how you would actually proceed.

**A.** You go through the standard procedure, keep the steps that still apply and adapt the rest, writing down why you changed each one.

**B.** You consult a colleague who has handled similar edge cases and ask how they dealt with it before acting.

**C.** You escalate to a supervisor with a short note explaining which part of the standard procedure doesn't fit and why.

**D.** You handle the case yourself and afterwards write it up so the procedure can be updated for next time.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q4.title: Cutting handling time without dropping steps
q4.body:
Average handling time must fall by 20% with the same staff and without cutting steps: you are asked which approach you would take.

**A.** You redesign the service flow so routine requests follow a shorter path and only complex cases go through every step.

**B.** You identify the slowest step and arrange for it to run in parallel with another one instead of waiting its turn.

**C.** You move some steps, such as confirmations or summaries, to an asynchronous follow-up after the call, so the live part is shorter.

**D.** You write templated responses for the most frequent requests so agents have more time for the complex ones.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q5.title: Speeding up your own incident response
q5.body:
Your team is slower than target on incidents and you are part of the reason: you are asked what you would do to get faster.

**A.** You shadow the fastest responder for a shift and note what they do in a different order or skip.

**B.** You review your last five incidents step by step and mark exactly where the minutes were lost.

**C.** You run simulated incidents against a timer and repeat them until your response time comes down.

**D.** You redesign your personal triage checklist, reordering or removing the items that actually slowed you down.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q6.title: How you build a staff schedule
q6.body:
You have to plan shifts for the team: the question asks what you would focus on first.

**A.** You model expected demand hour by hour, using past volumes, and place people where the load is.

**B.** You account for the skill mix on each shift, so every slot has someone who can handle the harder requests.

**C.** You plan buffers for spikes, keeping extra people or on-call cover for the hours when volume jumps.

**D.** You review constraints and rules first: contracts, rest periods, leave and legal limits.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q7.title: An upset customer who has the facts wrong
q7.body:
A customer is escalating a complaint: they are wrong about the facts but did have a poor experience. You are asked how you would respond.

**A.** You acknowledge their frustration, then set out what actually happened with times and specifics.

**B.** You focus the reply on the fact that the outcome fell short, leave the sequence of events aside and propose a resolution.

**C.** You ask the customer to confirm specific details of what happened, so any factual errors surface through their own answers.

**D.** You respond in writing with an apology and a resolution, then offer a phone call to go through the details.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q8.title: Two colleagues, two opposite pieces of advice
q8.body:
Two experienced colleagues tell you to handle a service situation in opposite ways: you are asked how you would decide.

**A.** You ask each of them to walk you through the reasoning behind their advice, not only what they would do.

**B.** You look at what is different about this situation compared with the times each approach worked before.

**C.** You try the approach whose downside is smaller if it goes wrong, then evaluate how it turned out.

**D.** You check whether there is a documented precedent for this kind of situation before choosing.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q9.title: A key component missing for three weeks
q9.body:
A supplier can't deliver a component you use daily for three weeks and you can't switch suppliers for good: you are asked what you would do.

**A.** You source a temporary alternative that is close enough and adjust your process to work with the differences.

**B.** You redesign the affected service workflow to run without the component for three weeks, with a different but acceptable experience for customers.

**C.** You negotiate partial or substitute deliveries with the supplier, asking first for the variants you need most urgently.

**D.** You build a small reserve by using less in lower-priority areas and moving that stock to the critical service lines.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q10.title: Outage scripts that customers find confusing
q10.body:
Customers say your team's outage explanations are confusing, and you wrote the scripts: you are asked how you would fix it.

**A.** You record real calls or messages and review them to pinpoint the sentences customers don't understand.

**B.** You rewrite the scripts in plain language and practise them on mock scenarios until they come out naturally.

**C.** You ask a communication trainer to observe one interaction and give you specific feedback.

**D.** You build a template library for the most common outage explanations and test it with a few users before rolling it out.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q11.title: Your go-to way of reducing errors
q11.body:
Errors keep occurring in the work and the question asks which method you would use first to bring them down.

**A.** You introduce checklists that people tick off at the key points of the task.

**B.** You standardize how the work is done and organize the workspace with 5S (sort, set in order, shine, standardize, sustain).

**C.** You automate repetitive steps, such as data entry or copying information, so they are no longer done by hand.

**D.** You trace each error back to where it starts, group errors by type and fix the cause at that step.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q12.title: Telling long-term clients service is being reduced
q12.body:
You must tell long-standing clients about a permanent cut in service level while keeping the relationship: you are asked how you would deliver the news.

**A.** You state the change plainly, with effective dates and the specific impact for each client segment.

**B.** You present the reduction as part of a wider service evolution that also brings improvements in other areas.

**C.** You contact the most impacted clients individually first, listen to their concerns and use them to shape the wider announcement.

**D.** You skip a mass announcement and hold individual account reviews, so each client hears the news in light of their own usage.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q13.title: Junior data that questions a trusted procedure
q13.body:
A junior colleague brings early case data suggesting a core assumption of a procedure you rely on is wrong: you are asked how you would react.

**A.** You pause the procedure in the affected cases and test both approaches on recent cases before choosing.

**B.** You go through the raw case data yourself to judge how solid it is before involving anyone else.

**C.** You log the challenge formally and continue with the procedure, setting a specific outcome threshold that would trigger a full review.

**D.** You ask two people who weren't involved in either analysis to evaluate the evidence independently.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q14.title: A self-service channel customers abandon
q14.body:
Management wants self-service to cut calls by 30%, but most customers who try it end up calling anyway: you are asked what you would propose.

**A.** You redesign the self-service flow to cover only the cases it resolves well and send complex cases to agents straight away.

**B.** You set up a hybrid where customers start in self-service and can hand over to an agent who already sees what they entered.

**C.** You reframe the target around repeat calls, using self-service for follow-ups and status checks.

**D.** You pilot three different self-service approaches on different case types to see which categories benefit before scaling up.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q15.title: Recurring gaps in your compliance documentation
q15.body:
An audit found the same gaps in your compliance documentation again and again: you are asked how you would build this skill.

**A.** You identify the two most common gaps and create a short personal checklist that covers exactly those points.

**B.** You ask the auditor to walk you through an example of what complete documentation looks like.

**C.** You put your documentation side by side with that of a colleague who scored well and note the differences.

**D.** You redo one recent document from scratch to the correct standard and time yourself while doing it.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q16.title: How you choose a new tool
q16.body:
You need to pick a new tool for the team: the question asks what you would rely on most to decide.

**A.** You list your requirements and score each candidate on how well it fits them.

**B.** You pilot the tool with a small group for a few weeks before deciding.

**C.** You weigh cost against expected benefit and look at the risks, such as lock-in or downtime.

**D.** You check how well it integrates with the systems you already use, such as your CRM or ticketing software.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q17.title: One training session for a mixed group
q17.body:
You have one session to train a group where half have related experience and half are beginners: you are asked how you would structure it.

**A.** You teach the whole workflow end to end at beginner level and offer an optional advanced session afterwards for experienced members.

**B.** You start with the conceptual model, why the workflow exists, and let each person connect it to what they already know.

**C.** You open with a short diagnostic exercise and then adjust the depth of each part to the gaps you find.

**D.** You pair experienced members with beginners, give them a guided practice scenario and move around answering questions.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q18.title: A new guideline against a proven practice
q18.body:
A new industry guideline, with limited but growing evidence, contradicts a practice your team has used for years: you are asked how you would respond.

**A.** You review the evidence behind the guideline and set it against your team's own outcome data.

**B.** You pilot the guideline on a subset of cases while the rest continue with the old practice for comparison.

**C.** You adopt the guideline and track outcomes closely to check it delivers what it claims.

**D.** You consult peers at other organizations to hear how they are interpreting and applying it.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q19.title: Extra paperwork at every shift handoff
q19.body:
A new regulation adds documentation at every shift handoff in a 24/7 operation, which would leave a 15-minute gap in coverage: you are asked how you would handle it.

**A.** You redesign the handoff format, replacing paper with a digital log that fills itself in from the shift's activity data.

**B.** You overlap shifts by 15 minutes and use that time for both the handoff and the documentation.

**C.** You split the requirement: critical items are captured during the handoff and detailed notes are written later in a quieter moment.

**D.** You work with compliance to define the minimum documentation that still satisfies the regulation.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q20.title: Backing your proposals with data
q20.body:
You have been told your process improvement proposals lack data: you are asked how you would build this skill.

**A.** You attach measurable baselines, such as current error rates or handling times, to your next proposal even if collecting them takes longer.

**B.** You partner with an analyst for a while to see how they build an argument around data.

**C.** You take a short course on operational data analysis and apply it straight away to a real improvement case.

**D.** You review three approved proposals to work out which data made them convincing.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

q21.title: How you judge a process change
q21.body:
You have to evaluate whether a process change worked: the question asks what you would rely on most.

**A.** You define the success metrics before the change starts, for example target handling time or error rate.

**B.** You compare the same data from before and after the change over similar periods.

**C.** You run a controlled trial, applying the change to one group and keeping another as it was.

**D.** You document the impact you observed and write down the next steps for the team.

There is no right answer: pick what you would really do most often.

open1.title: A service process you improved
open1.body:
Pick one real process you changed and walk through it:

- what the process was and what wasn't working
- what you changed and why
- what you did so the change lasted (training, checks, follow-up)
- what the result was, with a figure if you have one

A few sentences are enough (at least 50 characters). There is no right answer: describe what actually happened.

open2.title: The operations skill you want to grow
open2.body:
Name one specific area of your operations work and explain:

- why it matters to you or your team right now
- the concrete steps you plan to take this year
- how you will know it is working (a result, a number, feedback)

A few sentences are enough (at least 50 characters). There is no right answer: write about the area you actually want to work on.
